claim: The adult primate visual system comprises a series of hierarchically organized areas.
source: The adult primate visual system comprises a series of hierarchically organized areas.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about primate visual system organization.

claim: Each cortical area contains a topographic map of visual space, with different areas extracting different kinds of information from the retinal input.
source: Each cortical area contains a topographic map of visual space, with different areas extracting different kinds of information from the retinal input.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cortical visual areas.

claim: Hierarchical, topographic organization is present at birth in the primate visual system.
source: We find that hierarchical, topographic organization is present at birth and therefore constitutes a proto-organization for the entire primate visual system.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by fMRI data from neonatal macaques.

claim: Within inferior temporal cortex, proto-organization was already present prior to the emergence of category selectivity.
source: Even within inferior temporal cortex, this proto-organization was already present, prior to the emergence of category selectivity (e.g., faces or scenes).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data showing retinotopic organization in IT before face-selective clusters emerge.

claim: Topographic organization provides the scaffolding for the subsequent development of visual cortex that commences at the onset of visual experience.
source: We propose that this topographic organization provides the scaffolding for the subsequent development of visual cortex that commences at the onset of visual experience
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: The adult primate visual system comprises a series of interconnected, topographically-organized areas arranged in two, dorsal and ventral, distributed hierarchies.
source: The adult primate visual system comprises a series of interconnected, topographically-organized areas arranged in two, dorsal and ventral, distributed hierarchies (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Ungerleider and Mishkin, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The global organization and functional properties of individual areas throughout cortex are similar across individuals.
source: This global organization, as well as the anatomical location and functional properties of individual areas throughout cortex, are similar across individuals, suggesting an early common program for the development of the visual system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about visual system organization across individuals.

claim: Patterns of correlated activity across occipital, temporal, and parietal cortices revealed the arealization of visual cortex in newborns.
source: In newborns, patterns of correlated activity across occipital, temporal, and parietal cortices revealed the arealization of visual cortex and the specialization of these areas into dorsal and ventral visual pathways.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI correlation data from neonatal macaques.

claim: Correlated activity between areas reflected the topographic organization of visual space (retinotopy) in newborns.
source: Correlated activity between areas reflected the topographic organization of visual space (retinotopy).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of fMRI data from neonatal macaques.

claim: The retinotopic organization within high-level visual areas emerged prior to other functional selectivity.
source: Further, the retinotopic organization within high-level visual areas emerged prior to other functional selectivity.
evidence: This is supported by data showing eccentricity representations in IT before face selectivity.

claim: Eccentricity representations in inferotemporal cortex (IT) were identified months before IT showed the adult-like clustered organization for face selectivity.
source: Specifically, we identified eccentricity representations in inferotemporal cortex (IT) months before IT showed the adult-like clustered organization for face selectivity.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal fMRI data from the same monkeys at different ages.

claim: Tuning for spatial frequency and low-level shape features such as curvature were present prior to the detection of category domain clusters in IT.
source: Tuning for spatial frequency and low-level shape features such as curvature were also present prior to the detection of category domain clusters in IT.
evidence: This is supported by spatial frequency and curvature mapping data from infant monkeys.

claim: Areal differentiation, hierarchical organization, low-level shape selectivity, and retinotopic organization of the entire visual system is present at birth.
source: These results show that areal differentiation, hierarchical organization, low-level shape selectivity, and retinotopic organization of the entire visual system is present at birth, and likely serve as the scaffold for subsequent activity-dependent modifications throughout visual cortex.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple types of fMRI data.

claim: During the first few weeks after birth, visually evoked responses were present only in the LGN and weakly in peripheral V1.
source: During the first few weeks after birth, visually evoked responses were present only in the LGN and weakly in peripheral V1 (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data from monkeys B1 and B2 at 10 and 18 days postnatal shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Correlated activity between visual areas was significant even in the first few weeks after birth.
source: In contrast to visually evoked responses, correlated activity between visual areas was significant even in these first few weeks, and clearly distinguished visual areas from the rest of cortex.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of resting-state fMRI data from neonatal macaques.

claim: The mean signal of V1 was strongly correlated with occipital, temporal, and posterior parietal cortices during non-visual-stimulation rest periods in neonates.
source: For example, the mean signal of V1 was strongly correlated with occipital, temporal, and posterior parietal cortices during non-visual-stimulation rest periods (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by correlation maps shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The extent of the V1 correlations in newborns covered the entire cortical visual system.
source: These maps were registered to the newborn data and confirmed that the extent of the V1 correlations in newborns covered the entire cortical visual system.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of neonatal correlation maps with retinotopic maps obtained later.

claim: The correspondence of the correlation maps to extrastriate visual areas was verified at about 1 month after birth when visually-evoked responses could be reliably measured throughout these extrastriate areas.
source: The correspondence of the correlation maps to extrastriate visual areas was further verified at about 1 month after birth when visually-evoked responses could be reliably measured throughout these extrastriate areas (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is supported by visually-evoked fMRI data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The lack of early visually-evoked fMRI activity may reflect differences between physiological and metabolic measurements.
source: Though the lack of early visually-evoked fMRI activity is in apparent contrast with previous electrophysiological findings that demonstrated visual responsiveness in infants (Rust et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2005; Endo et al., 2000), this may reflect differences between physiological and metabolic measurements as a similar lack of early activity has been observed using deoxyglucose (Distler et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous studies using different methods.

claim: The apparent dissociation between the absence of visually-evoked activations and the presence of V1-correlated activity may reflect population-level immaturity of the visual pathway or a low-arousal state in neonatal monkeys.
source: As such, the apparent dissociation between the absence of visually-evoked activations and the presence of V1-correlated activity (Figure 1a and b) may reflect population-level immaturity of the visual pathway (Distler et al., 1996; Bachevalier et al., 1991) or a low-arousal state in these neonatal monkeys.
evidence: This is speculation based on previous research and the authors' observations.

claim: Several visual cortical ICs were identified in B1 and B2, at 10 and 18 days old respectively, comprising foveal or peripheral occipital cortex, dorsal extrastriate, posterior parietal, middle temporal (MT), and IT cortex.
source: Similar to these findings in adults, several visual cortical ICs were identified in B1 and B2, at 10 and 18 days old respectively, comprising foveal or peripheral occipital cortex, dorsal extrastriate, posterior parietal, middle temporal (MT), and IT cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by independent component analysis (ICA) of fMRI data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spatial maps for each IC were bilateral and symmetric, encompassing comparable regions between hemispheres.
source: Spatial maps for each IC were bilateral and symmetric, encompassing comparable regions between hemispheres.
evidence: This is an observation from the ICA analysis of neonatal fMRI data.

claim: Functionally specific regional differentiation, both of the entire visual system and even within the visual system, was already present in newborn macaques.
source: These data further indicate that functionally specific regional differentiation, both of the entire visual system and even within the visual system, was already present in newborn macaques.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ICA analysis of neonatal fMRI data.

claim: There were ICs in neonatal data within somatomotor, auditory, frontal, and parietal cortices, as well as within the thalamus.
source: Also, as in adults, there were ICs in these neonatal data within somatomotor, auditory, frontal, and parietal cortices, as well as within the thalamus, demonstrating regionally-specific signals throughout sensory and association regions in the newborn brain.
evidence: This is supported by ICA analysis of neonatal fMRI data.

claim: Individual visual areas across occipital, temporal, and parietal cortices could be distinguished at birth using seed-based correlation analysis.
source: Even individual visual areas across occipital, temporal, and parietal cortices could be distinguished at birth using seed-based correlation analysis.
evidence: This is supported by across-hemisphere correlation analysis of neonatal fMRI data.

claim: Previous anatomical studies in primates have shown callosal connections between the same visual areas in opposite hemispheres (homotopic) in adult and infant primates.
source: Previous anatomical studies in primates have shown callosal connections between the same visual areas in opposite hemispheres, that is, homotopic, in adult (Abel et al., 2000; Kennedy et al., 1986) and infant (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Kennedy et al., 1986; Underleider and Mishkin, 1982; Maunsell and van Essen, 1983; Van Essen et al., 1982; Kaas, 1995; Dehay et al., 1986; Baldwin et al., 2012) primates
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Callosal connections are correlated with areal and hierarchical organization.
source: and these callosal connections are correlated with areal and hierarchical organization (Kennedy et al., 1986; Maunsell and van Essen, 1983; Van Essen et al., 1982; Kaas, 1995; Schmidt, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous fMRI studies in adult humans and monkeys have shown homotopic correlations.
source: Consistent with these anatomical studies, previous fMRI studies in adult humans and monkeys have shown homotopic correlations (Moeller et al., 2009; Biswal et al., 1995; Vincent et al., 2007; Butt et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous fMRI studies.

claim: Homotopic correlations are mediated by callosal connections.
source: which are mediated by callosal connections (Johnston et al., 2008; O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mean signals between homotopic cortical areas were significantly correlated in each monkey across all 16 cortical areas tested.
source: Across all 16 cortical areas tested, mean signals between homotopic cortical areas were significantly correlated in each monkey (ts(15)>18.07; ps<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data from neonatal macaques.

claim: The strength of correlation varied as a function of areal group.
source: The strength of correlation varied as a function of areal group (2-way ANOVA with monkey and areal grouping as factors; ps<0.01; Figure 2 legend).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data.

claim: Pairwise correlations were strongest between homotopic cortical areas, followed by cortical areas neighboring homotopic regions, and then cortical areas distal, non-neighboring to homotopic regions.
source: Across all 16 areas tested, pairwise correlations were strongest between homotopic cortical areas, followed by cortical areas neighboring homotopic regions, and then cortical areas distal, non-neighboring to homotopic regions (two-tailed, unpaired t-tests; Homotopic vs. Adjacent: t(134) = 3.96; Adjacent vs. Distal: t(478) > 10.27; ps<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data from neonatal macaques.

claim: Across hemisphere correlations from simulated data were not significantly different from 0.
source: Across hemisphere correlations from these simulated data were not significantly different from 0 (Figure 2b; grey box plots).
evidence: This is supported by control analysis using simulated data.

claim: Potential biases from instrumentation affected only within-hemisphere correlations for neighboring areas, and even then could not fully account for the observed correlation structure.
source: This control analysis also revealed that such potential biases affected only within-hemisphere correlations for neighboring areas, and even then could not fully account for the observed correlation structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the control analysis using simulated data.

claim: Significant across-hemisphere voxel-wise correlations were observed for all 16 seed areas in each monkey.
source: We observed significant across-hemisphere voxel-wise correlations for all 16 seed areas in each monkey (r > 0.15; t > 5.66; p<0.0001, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This is supported by voxel-wise correlation analysis of neonatal fMRI data.

claim: Voxel-wise correlations were almost exclusively within the extent of visual cortex and peak correlations were within each seed's homotopic cortical area.
source: Voxel-wise correlations were almost exclusively within the extent of visual cortex and peak correlations were within each seed's homotopic cortical area (e.g., across-hemisphere correlations for area MT in left hemisphere were strongest with right-hemisphere voxels in MT; Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by voxel-wise correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Across the 16 seed cortical areas, across-hemisphere areal correlation profiles were strongest for voxels within the homotopic area, with areal correlation profile strength dropping off with distance.
source: Across the 16 seed cortical areas, across-hemisphere areal correlation profiles were strongest for voxels within the homotopic area, with areal correlation profile strength dropping off with distance (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is supported by areal correlation profile analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Within-hemisphere areal correlation profile maps were comparable to the across-hemisphere maps for matched seed areas.
source: Within-hemisphere areal correlation profile maps were comparable to the across-hemisphere maps for matched seed areas (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of within- and across-hemisphere correlation maps.

claim: Arealization of the entire visual hierarchy already existed within the first weeks after birth.
source: Taken together, these areal correlation profile maps further demonstrated that arealization of the entire visual hierarchy already existed within the first weeks after birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the areal correlation profile analysis.

claim: Community structure analyses of neonatal correlation patterns revealed a large-scale organization of the visual system into dorsal and ventral visual subdivisions.
source: Community structure analyses of neonatal correlation patterns revealed a large-scale organization of the visual system into dorsal and ventral visual subdivisions, as is found in adult monkeys (Ungerleider and Mishkin, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by multidimensional scaling and community structure analysis of neonatal correlation data.

claim: Multidimensional scaling of the neonatal across-hemisphere correlations revealed the two principle dimensions of structure: posterior-anterior and dorsal-ventral.
source: Multidimensional scaling of the neonatal across-hemisphere (temporal) correlations between 16 visual cortical areas (Figure 2a), revealed the two principle dimensions of structure: posterior-anterior and dorsal-ventral (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by multidimensional scaling analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The cortical location of an area was a good predictor of its connectivity in neonates.
source: This indicates that the cortical location of an area was a good predictor of its connectivity; this is similar to what has been found in adult monkeys using within-hemisphere anatomical connections (Young, 1992; Markov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference from the multidimensional scaling analysis, compared with previous studies in adults.

claim: Spectral community structure analysis of neonatal correlations partitioned 16 cortical areas into 3 groups: occipital areas V1, V2, and V3; ventral temporal areas V4, V4A, OTd, PITv, PITd, and OTS; and dorsal areas V3A/DP, CIP, LIP, as well as the MT cluster.
source: Spectral community structure analysis of neonatal correlations partitioned these 16 cortical areas into 3 groups: (1) occipital areas V1, V2, and V3 (green dots), (2) ventral temporal areas V4, V4A, OTd, PITv, PITd, and OTS (red dots), and (3) dorsal areas V3A/DP, CIP, LIP, as well as the MT cluster (blue dots).
evidence: This is supported by spectral community structure analysis of neonatal correlation data.

claim: MT was functionally grouped with dorsal stream areas despite its anatomical location in temporal cortex and proximity to ventral stream areas.
source: Consistent with the organization found in adult monkeys, MT was functionally grouped with dorsal stream areas despite its anatomical location in temporal cortex and proximity to ventral stream areas V4, OTd, and PIT (Ungerleider and Mishkin, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by community structure analysis and comparison with adult organization.

claim: Occipital cortical areas were correlated with both ventral and dorsal groups.
source: Occipital cortical areas were correlated with both ventral and dorsal groups.
evidence: This is an observation from the community structure analysis.

claim: Correlations between dorsal and ventral groups were present, though relatively weak compared to correlations within groups.
source: Correlations between dorsal and ventral groups were also present, though relatively weak compared to correlations within groups.
evidence: This is an observation from the correlation analysis.

claim: There is a clear distinction, at birth, between dorsal and ventral visual pathways, which is similar to the known organization of the adult visual system.
source: This analysis thus yielded a clear distinction, at birth, between dorsal and ventral visual pathways, which is similar to the known organization of the adult visual system.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the community structure analysis, compared with adult organization.

claim: Hierarchical cluster analysis revealed nested layers within the functional segregation of dorsal and ventral pathways at birth.
source: Hierarchical cluster analysis revealed nested layers within the functional segregation of dorsal and ventral pathways at birth (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: V1 was situated in the middle of the dendrogram with one set of areas extending into inferior temporal cortex and other areas extending into parietal cortex.
source: V1 was situated in the middle of the dendrogram with one set of areas (left) extending into inferior temporal cortex and other areas (right) extending into parietal cortex.
evidence: This is an observation from the hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: Hierarchical clustering resulted in a finer-grained parcellation into five clusters: posterior occipital areas V1, V2, and V3; anterior occipital areas V4, V4A, and OTd; inferior temporal areas PITd, PITv, and OTS; the MT cluster; and dorsal areas V3A, CIP, LIP.
source: Hierarchical clustering resulted in a finer-grained parcellation into five clusters: posterior occipital areas V1, V2, and V3 (green), anterior occipital areas V4, V4A, and OTd (peach), inferior temporal areas PITd, PITv, and OTS (red), the MT cluster (cyan), and dorsal areas V3A, CIP, LIP (blue).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of neonatal correlation data.

claim: The multidimensional scaling and hierarchical clustering revealed the presence, at birth, of the well-established (in adults) broad differentiation between dorsal and ventral visual pathways as well as a hierarchical organization within each pathway.
source: Taken together, the multidimensional scaling and hierarchical clustering revealed the presence, at birth, of the well-established (in adults) broad differentiation between dorsal and ventral visual pathways as well as a hierarchical organization within each pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the community structure and hierarchical clustering analyses.

claim: A series of retinotopic representations could be inferred from correlation patterns in neonatal visual areas.
source: An even finer level of differentiation within individual neonatal visual areas was apparent as a series of retinotopic representations that could be inferred from correlation patterns.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of neonatal fMRI data.

claim: Within-hemisphere correlations between dorsal or ventral quadrant pairs were stronger than correlations between non-matched quadrant pairs.
source: Within-hemisphere correlations between dorsal or ventral quadrant pairs (e.g., dorsal V1 and dorsal V2) were stronger than correlations between non-matched quadrant pairs (2-way ANOVA; main effects of quadrant group: F(1,156) = 45.1, p<0.0001; marginal effect of monkey F(1,156)=3.63, p<0.06; no interaction p>0.10)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of within-hemisphere correlation data.

claim: The mean signals of homotopic quadrants across hemispheres were significantly correlated in each monkey.
source: The mean signals of homotopic quadrants across hemispheres were significantly correlated in each monkey (ts(9)>17.21; ps<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of across-hemisphere correlation data.

claim: The homotopic correlations were stronger for corresponding dorsal or ventral quadrants than for non-corresponding quadrants.
source: The checkerboard pattern of the correlation matrix in Figure 6a indicates that the homotopic correlations were stronger for corresponding dorsal or ventral quadrants than for non-corresponding quadrants (Figure 6b; 2-way ANOVA with monkey and quadrant group as factors; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Across-hemisphere correlations between non-homotopic regions were greater for corresponding dorsal or ventral quadrants than for non-corresponding quadrants.
source: Across-hemisphere correlations between non-homotopic regions were also greater for corresponding dorsal or ventral quadrants (e.g., dorsal V1 right hemisphere to dorsal V3 left hemisphere) than for non-corresponding quadrants (2-way ANOVA; main effect of quadrant group: F(1,92) = 10.87, p<0.0014; no main effect of monkey, p>0.10; no interaction between monkey and quadrant group, p>0.10).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of across-hemisphere correlation data.

claim: Dorsal:dorsal and ventral:ventral correlations were stronger than dorsal:ventral correlations even across areas, likely reflecting the underlying topographic organization within each area.
source: Because dorsal:dorsal and ventral:ventral correlations were stronger than dorsal:ventral correlations even across areas (e.g., V1 to V3), these correlations likely reflect the underlying topographic organization within each area, not solely mirror symmetrical point-to-point connections between hemispheres.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation data about the nature of the organization.

claim: Callosal connections linking neurons with overlapping receptive fields at or near the vertical meridian can account for correlated activity between hemispheres in adults.
source: Even though right and left hemispheres represent left and right visual fields, respectively, callosal connections linking neurons with overlapping receptive fields at or near the vertical meridian (Dehay et al., 1986) can account for correlated activity between hemispheres in adults (Heinzle et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A coarse topographic organization within individual areas of newborn monkeys likely reflects retinotopic organization.
source: These data demonstrate a coarse topographic organization within individual areas of newborn monkeys that likely reflects retinotopic organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the quadrant correlation analysis.

claim: The IC analysis revealed a broad foveal vs. peripheral distinction in neonates.
source: The IC analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) had revealed a broad foveal vs. peripheral distinction
evidence: This is supported by ICA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The checkerboard pattern of correlations between dorsal vs. ventral subdivisions of individual occipital areas indicated a lower vs. upper visual-field specificity.
source: and the checkerboard pattern of correlations between dorsal vs. ventral subdivisions of individual occipital areas (Figure 6) indicated a lower vs. upper visual-field specificity.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Within-hemisphere correlated activity patterns at early age reflected the retinotopic organization measured in the same monkeys much later in life.
source: We then asked how detailed this retinotopic organization was across visual cortex. At this age, we could not perform conventional retinotopic mapping. Instead, we evaluated whether within-hemisphere correlated activity patterns at this early age reflected the retinotopic organization measured in the same monkeys much later in life (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of neonatal correlation maps with later retinotopic mapping.

claim: The eccentricity correlation maps obtained in neonates were predictive of the eccentricity organization derived by direct retinotopic mapping in the same monkeys when they were older.
source: The resulting eccentricity correlation maps obtained in neonates were predictive of the eccentricity organization derived by direct retinotopic mapping in the same monkeys when they were older and able to fixate continuously with high accuracy (within 1°) for several minutes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of neonatal eccentricity correlation maps with later retinotopic mapping shown in Figure 7.

claim: Lateral occipital cortex had foveal correlations in neonates that extended anteriorly along the lower lip of the STS.
source: Specifically, lateral occipital cortex had foveal correlations in neonates that extended anteriorly along the lower lip of the STS.
evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis.

claim: Moving towards the medial occipital surface, eccentricity correlations gradually shifted towards the periphery.
source: Moving towards the medial occipital surface, eccentricity correlations gradually shifted towards the periphery.
evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis.

claim: A region of foveal correlation, distinct from the foveal confluence of early visual cortex, was present within the fundus of the STS, corresponding to what later could be identified as the fovea of the MT cluster.
source: A region of foveal correlation, distinct from the foveal confluence of early visual cortex, was present within the fundus of the STS, corresponding to what later could be identified as the fovea of the MT cluster.
evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis, compared with later mapping.

claim: Parafoveal and peripheral correlations encircled the MT fovea, especially in the dorsal-most portions of the STS near the prelunate gyrus and crown of the IPS, consistent with the retinotopic organization identified when the monkeys were older.
source: Parafoveal and peripheral correlations encircled this fovea, especially in the dorsal-most portions of the STS near the prelunate gyrus and crown of the IPS; consistent with the retinotopic organization identified when the monkeys were older.
evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis, compared with later mapping.

claim: The mean absolute deviation between eccentricity correlations in newborns and the eccentricity measurements from retinotopic mapping after 1.5 years of age was 2.2° across all retinotopic areas (excluding V1).
source: Excluding V1 (i.e., the seed area), the mean absolute deviation between eccentricity correlations in newborns and the eccentricity measurements from retinotopic mapping after 1.5 years of age was 2.2° across all retinotopic areas, in both hemispheres, in both monkeys.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of neonatal correlation maps with later retinotopic mapping.

claim: Actual V1 correlations with V2 and V3 were approximately 2x and 5x, respectively, greater than estimated correlations attributable to spatial spread of the fMRI signal.
source: Actual V1 correlations with V2 and V3 were approximately 2x and 5x, respectively, greater than estimated correlations attributable to spatial spread of the fMRI signal.
evidence: This is a comparison of actual correlations with simulated correlations from spatial spread.

claim: Anterior to V3, correlations with V1 in the simulation were negligible.
source: Anterior to V3, correlations with V1 in our simulation were negligible.
evidence: This is a result from the simulation analysis.

claim: The neonate eccentricity correlation maps were similar to correlation maps obtained in the same monkeys as juveniles (~3 years of age).
source: The neonate eccentricity correlation maps were also similar to correlation maps obtained in the same monkeys as juveniles (~3 years of age), indicating that retinotopic correlation patterns are present through development.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of neonatal and juvenile correlation maps.

claim: The mean absolute deviation between eccentricity correlations at newborn and juvenile ages was 2.0° across retinotopic areas (excluding V1).
source: Excluding V1, the mean absolute deviation between eccentricity correlations at newborn and juvenile ages was 2.0° across retinotopic areas, in both hemispheres, in both monkeys.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of neonatal and juvenile correlation maps.

claim: Juvenile eccentricity correlations were more similar to the eccentricity mapping (mean deviation = 1.4°) than to the neonate eccentricity correlations.
source: Juvenile eccentricity correlations were more similar to the eccentricity mapping (mean deviation = 1.4°) than to the neonate eccentricity correlations, potentially indicating refinement of retinotopic maps over development.
evidence: This is a comparison of juvenile correlations with both neonatal correlations and later mapping, suggesting developmental refinement.

claim: Extensive retinotopic organization across both early and higher visual cortex was already present within the first weeks of life.
source: These data indicate that extensive retinotopic organization across both early and higher visual cortex was already present within the first weeks of life.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the eccentricity correlation analysis.

claim: Early eccentricity maps extended into regions of IT cortex that in adults are organized into domains selectively responsive to different object categories, like faces.
source: These early eccentricity maps extended into regions of IT cortex that in adults are organized into domains selectively responsive to different object categories, like faces (Tsao et al., 2003; Pinsk et al., 2009; Bell et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis, compared with adult organization.

claim: Regions of IT selectively responsive to face and non-face stimuli (measured with fMRI) were not differentiable in IT cortex at young age.
source: At this young age, however, regions of IT selectively responsive to face and non-face stimuli (measured with fMRI) were not differentiable in IT cortex (Livingstone et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a previous study from the same lab.

claim: Face patches would not emerge until about 200 days in these monkeys.
source: Face patches would not emerge until about 200 days in these monkeys (Figure 8a, thick black outline).
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal fMRI data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: Foveal biases were identified in neonatal data along the lower lip of the STS, including a region that would eventually be identifiable as the middle face patch (ML).
source: Yet foveal biases were identified in this neonatal data along the lower lip of the STS, including a region that would eventually be identifiable as the middle face patch (ML), consistent with previous studies that compared eccentricity and face patch organization in adult monkeys (Janssens et al., 2014; Rajimehr et al., 2014; Lafer-Sousa and Conway, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by eccentricity correlation analysis and comparison with previous studies.

claim: In neonates, the eccentricity correlations within what would become area ML were mostly foveal, though midfield and peripheral representations were identified on the medial edge within the fundus in 3 of 4 hemispheres.
source: In neonates, the eccentricity correlations within what would become area ML were mostly foveal, though midfield and peripheral representations were identified on the medial edge within the fundus in 3 of 4 hemispheres.
evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis in the precursor-ML region.

claim: The progression of eccentricity representations in the precursor-ML region was consistent with eccentricity representations from subsequent mapping in these same monkeys at >1.5 years of age, and with a previous study in adult monkeys.
source: This progression of eccentricity representations was consistent with eccentricity representations from subsequent mapping in these same monkeys at >1.5 years of age, and with a previous study in adult monkeys (Janssens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with later mapping and previous studies.

claim: Correlations of the region that would become ML were strongest with the most foveal V1 bin and diminished towards the periphery.
source: Correlations of the region that would become ML were strongest with the most foveal V1 bin and diminished towards the periphery (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of correlations between precursor-ML and V1 eccentricity bins shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The pattern of V1 eccentricity correlations in neonates paralleled the distribution of eccentricity representations in ML from subsequent retinotopic mapping in these same monkeys at >1.5 years; both showed an overall foveal bias.
source: The pattern of V1 eccentricity correlations in neonates paralleled the distribution of eccentricity representations in ML from subsequent retinotopic mapping in these same monkeys at >1.5 years; both of which showed an overall foveal bias (Figure 8b and c).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of neonatal correlations with later retinotopic mapping shown in Figure 8b and c.

claim: The anterior face patch (AL) showed a bimodal retinotopic correlation pattern, with the strongest correlations at foveal- and peripheral-most V1 bins.
source: Though eccentricity representations were weak in the most anterior parts of IT, the anterior face patch (AL) showed a bimodal retinotopic correlation pattern, with the strongest correlations at foveal- and peripheral-most V1 bins, consistent with the sub-threshold distribution of eccentricity representations mapped >1.5 years later (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of correlations in the precursor-AL region shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Retinotopic organization of what would become category-selective regions in IT cortex was already established within the first weeks after birth.
source: Together, these data indicate that retinotopic organization of what would become category-selective regions in IT cortex was already established within the first weeks after birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of eccentricity correlations in precursor face-patch regions.

claim: Neonatal correlation patterns did not reveal a face-patch organization.
source: Though neonatal correlation patterns distinguished retinotopic areas within IT (Figures 2 and 4) and neonatal ICA analysis revealed a broad IT component (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), neither analysis revealed a face-patch organization in neonates.
evidence: This is an observation from the correlation and ICA analyses of neonatal data.

claim: Task-evoked face-selective clusters in IT do not appear until about 200 days of age.
source: These data are consistent with a recent study from our lab showing that task-evoked face-selective clusters in IT do not appear until about 200 days of age (Livingstone et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a previous study from the same lab.

claim: After 200 days of age both IC analysis and univariate analysis revealed face patches; before 200 days neither showed face-patch organization.
source: After 200 days of age both IC analysis and univariate analysis revealed face patches; before 200 days neither showed face-patch organization. (Figure 8—figure supplement 2) (Livingstone et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by ICA analysis at different ages shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and a previous study.

claim: Foveal and peripheral ICs were identified in older datasets, demonstrating the stability of retinotopic organization through development.
source: In these older datasets, foveal and peripheral ICs were also identified, further demonstrating the stability of retinotopic organization through development.
evidence: This is an observation from ICA analysis at different ages.

claim: For datasets from monkeys older than 200 days, IC components comprising the face patch system also included foveal and parafoveal (~1°−6°) regions of occipital cortex.
source: For datasets from monkeys older than 200 days, IC components comprising the face patch system also included foveal and parafoveal (~1°−6°) regions of occipital cortex, demonstrating that the link between retinotopy and category selective domains is consistent through development.
evidence: This is an observation from ICA analysis of older monkeys.

claim: The retinotopic areal organization in inferior temporal cortex precedes category selectivity.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the retinotopic areal organization in inferior temporal cortex precedes category selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the longitudinal analysis of retinotopic organization and face selectivity.

claim: In adult monkeys, receptive-field size and preferred stimulus size scale with eccentricity.
source: In adult monkeys, receptive-field size and preferred stimulus size scale with eccentricity (Hubel and Wiesel, 1974)
evidence: This is established knowledge about adult visual system organization, supported by citation.

claim: Smaller receptive fields in the fovea prefer high spatial frequencies and short or curved contours; peripheral receptive fields are tuned to lower spatial frequencies and longer straight contours.
source: smaller receptive fields in the fovea prefer high spatial frequencies and short or curved contours; peripheral receptive fields are tuned to lower spatial frequencies and longer straight contours (Hubel and Wiesel, 1965; De Valois et al., 1982).
evidence: This is established knowledge about receptive field properties, supported by citations.

claim: In adults, maps of both spatial frequency and curvature tuning correlate with eccentricity maps.
source: Therefore, in adults, maps of both spatial frequency and curvature tuning correlate with eccentricity maps (Ponce et al., 2017; Srihasam et al., 2014; Henriksson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Spatial frequency mapping was performed in one infant monkey at 110 days old, well after significant visual responses had appeared with fMRI, but prior to the emergence of face-selective clusters in IT.
source: To see whether the eccentricity organization we found in neonates carried with it a similar selectivity for stimulus scale, we performed spatial frequency mapping in one infant monkey at 110 days old, well after significant visual responses had appeared with fMRI (Figure 1), but prior to the emergence of face-selective clusters in IT (Figure 8a).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and timing of the spatial frequency mapping.

claim: Preferred spatial frequency varied as a function of both visual hierarchy and eccentricity in infants.
source: As in adults, preferred spatial frequency varied as a function of both visual hierarchy and eccentricity (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is supported by spatial frequency mapping data shown in Figure 9a.

claim: In each area, foveal regions preferred the highest spatial frequencies and peripheral regions lower spatial frequencies.
source: In particular, in each area, foveal regions preferred the highest spatial frequencies and peripheral regions lower spatial frequencies (Figure 9b–d).
evidence: This is supported by spatial frequency mapping data shown in Figure 9b-d.

claim: The mean preferred spatial frequency decreased moving up the hierarchy, in both dorsal and ventral pathways.
source: In addition, the mean preferred spatial frequency decreased moving up the hierarchy, in both dorsal and ventral pathways (Figure 9d).
evidence: This is supported by spatial frequency mapping data shown in Figure 9d.

claim: There is a correlation between eccentricity and spatial frequency in infants prior to the emergence of category selectivity.
source: Thus, although we could not do spatial frequency mapping in neonatal monkeys, we nevertheless did observe a correlation between eccentricity and spatial frequency in infants that were slightly older but still prior to the emergence of category selectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the spatial frequency mapping in 110-day-old infant.

claim: The presence of retinotopy, as measured by correlation patterns in the neonates, implies a corresponding early organization for receptive field scale.
source: We therefore assume that the presence of retinotopy, as measured by correlation patterns in the neonates, implies a corresponding early organization for receptive field scale.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between retinotopy and spatial frequency tuning.

claim: Curvature selectivity varies with eccentricity in adult monkeys.
source: Because curvature selectivity varies with eccentricity in adult monkeys (Ponce et al., 2017; Srihasam et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Responses to curved and rectilinear stimuli were measured in monkey B4 at 186 days.
source: Responses to curved and rectilinear stimuli were measured in monkey B4 at 186 days (Figure 10).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for curvature mapping.

claim: 186 days is around the age when face-selective clusters first emerge.
source: This is around the age when face-selective clusters first emerge (Livingstone et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a previous study from the same lab.

claim: Curvature tuning varied as a function of both area and eccentricity in infants.
source: Similar to spatial frequency, curvature tuning varied as a function of both area and eccentricity (Figure 10b–e).
evidence: This is supported by curvature mapping data shown in Figure 10b-e.

claim: Only V1-V4A, OTd, and PITd showed significant selectivity for curvature.
source: Only V1-V4A, OTd, and PITd showed significant selectivity for curvature
evidence: This is an observation from the curvature mapping data.

claim: In areas V1-V4A, OTd, and PITd, foveal regions preferred curved stimuli more than rectilinear, and peripheral regions either showed no preference or preferred rectilinear stimuli.
source: and in each of these areas foveal regions preferred curved stimuli more than rectilinear, and peripheral regions either showed no preference or preferred rectilinear stimuli (Figure 10c–d).
evidence: This is supported by curvature mapping data shown in Figure 10c-d.

claim: An organization for curvature tuning is present at least as early as the time in development that face clusters emerge.
source: Therefore an organization for curvature tuning is present at least as early as the time in development that face clusters emerge.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the curvature mapping at 186 days.

claim: Area PITv showed a correlation between curvature and eccentricity, but also showed stronger average selectivity for rectilinear stimuli.
source: Area PITv showed a correlation between curvature and eccentricity, but in addition showed stronger average selectivity for rectilinear stimuli.
evidence: This is an observation from the curvature mapping data.

claim: V3A/DP showed stronger average selectivity for rectilinear stimuli.
source: V3A/DP also showed stronger average selectivity for rectilinear stimuli.
evidence: This is an observation from the curvature mapping data.

claim: PITv and V3A/DP correspond to scene-selective cortex.
source: These two regions correspond to scene-selective cortex (Nasr et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PITv and V3A/DP have been shown to prefer rectilinear stimuli also in adults.
source: and have been shown to prefer rectilinear stimuli also in adults (Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: OTS (combined areas OTS1 and OTS2) showed stronger average selectivity for rectilinear stimuli.
source: OTS (combined areas OTS1 and OTS2) also showed stronger average selectivity for rectilinear stimuli.
evidence: This is an observation from the curvature mapping data.

claim: OTS1 and OTS2 are located in a region of the occipitotemporal sulcus that likely corresponds to the scene area LPP.
source: OTS1 and OTS2 are located in a region of the occipitotemporal sulcus that likely corresponds to the scene area LPP (Arcaro and Livingstone, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research from the same authors.

claim: The scene area LPP prefers rectilinear stimuli in adults.
source: which also prefers rectilinear stimuli in adults (Kornblith et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: An organization for low-level shape selectivity precedes category selectivity, and contributes to the formation of category-selective domains.
source: Thus, it seems likely that an organization for low-level shape selectivity precedes category selectivity, and contributes to the formation of category-selective domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the spatial frequency and curvature mapping data.

claim: The visual system was organized to a remarkable degree in newborn macaques as young as 10 days postnatal.
source: The visual system was found to be organized to a remarkable degree in newborn macaques as young as 10 days postnatal.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: Visual cortex was functionally distinct from other sensory and non-sensory regions in newborns.
source: Visual cortex was functionally distinct from other sensory and non-sensory regions.
evidence: This is supported by correlation and ICA analyses of neonatal fMRI data.

claim: Across-hemisphere correlations revealed arealization and a hierarchical organization in newborns that was similar to that seen in adults.
source: Across-hemisphere correlations revealed arealization and a hierarchical organization that was similar to that seen in adults.
evidence: This is supported by correlation and community structure analyses of neonatal data.

claim: Correlations between areas were retinotopically organized in newborns.
source: Correlations between areas were retinotopically organized.
evidence: This is supported by eccentricity correlation analysis of neonatal data.

claim: The data provide the developmentally earliest account of the global functional organization of the visual system.
source: Our data provide the developmentally earliest account of the global functional organization of the visual system
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: The data demonstrate substrates for the adult organization across the whole visual system, not just thalamo-receipient V1.
source: and demonstrate substrates for the adult organization across the whole visual system, not just thalamo-receipient V1 as shown previously (Coogan and Van Essen, 1996; Horton and Hocking, 1997; Burkhalter et al., 1993; Blasdel et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a claim about the scope of the findings compared to previous work.

claim: Areal distinctions and retinotopy were present throughout visual cortex at 10 days of age.
source: Areal distinctions and retinotopy were present throughout visual cortex in our earliest data; 10 days of age.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the earliest data.

claim: It is unlikely that the organization emerged postnatally as a result of visually driven activity.
source: It is unlikely that this organization emerged postnatally as a result of visually driven activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the early presence of organization and the rate of axonal growth.

claim: The wiring of visual cortex needed to support the results most certainly began prenatally, given the rate of axonal growth (0.4–1.4 mm/day).
source: Given the rate of axonal growth (0.4–1.4 mm/day) (Lallemend et al., 2012), the wiring of visual cortex needed to support our results most certainly began prenatally.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rate of axonal growth and the timing of the observed organization.

claim: Adult-like organization is evident later in gestation and within the first weeks of birth.
source: and that adult-like organization is evident later in gestation (Coogan and Van Essen, 1996; Killackey and Chalupa, 1986; Barone et al., 1996; Batardière et al., 2002) as well as within the first weeks of birth (Baldwin et al., 2012; Horton and Hocking, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The large-scale organization of the visual system throughout ventral temporal and dorsal parietal cortex is established prenatally, prior to visual experience.
source: By measuring functional organization of the whole visual system at once, we show that the large-scale organization of the visual system throughout ventral temporal and dorsal parietal cortex is established prenatally, prior to visual experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the findings about early organization.

claim: How retinotopic maps are established must involve a combination of molecular cues and activity-dependent sorting.
source: How these maps are established is beyond the scope of this study, but must involve a combination of molecular cues and activity-dependent sorting (McLaughlin and O'Leary, 2005; Rosa, 2002).
evidence: This is speculation about mechanisms, supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Functional organization was apparent at birth throughout the visual system, even though the visual system is still anatomically and functionally immature by several criteria.
source: Functional organization was apparent at birth throughout the visual system, even though the visual system is still anatomically and functionally immature by several criteria.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the apparent paradox of early organization despite immaturity.

claim: There is no consensus on what would define a 'mature' visual area.
source: There is no consensus on what would define a 'mature' visual area—anatomy, physiology, connectivity, size, or malleability?
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of consensus in the field.

claim: In neonates, V1 exhibits a high degree of adult-like connectivity, impressive adult-like modular organization and precise adult-like selectivity to visual features.
source: In neonates, V1 exhibits a high degree of adult-like connectivity (Coogan and Van Essen, 1996; Horton and Hocking, 1997; Burkhalter et al., 1993), impressive adult-like modular organization (Blasdel et al., 1995) and precise adult-like selectivity to visual features (Wiesel and Hubel, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: V1 is clearly immature at birth, given how dramatically modifiable young (but not adult) V1 is by postnatal visual experience.
source: Yet V1 is clearly immature at birth, given how dramatically modifiable young (but not adult) V1 is by postnatal visual experience (Wiesel, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on critical periods.

claim: Studies in infant extrastriate cortex showing adult-like physiological properties and connectivity should not be interpreted as proving that these areas are mature and unmodifiable by experience.
source: Therefore studies in infant extrastriate cortex showing adult-like physiological properties and connectivity (Rodman et al., 1993a, 1993b) should not be interpreted as proving that these areas are mature and unmodifiable by experience.
evidence: This is an inference about how to interpret previous studies, based on the V1 example.

claim: There is evidence that both the physiology and anatomy of the extrastriate visual system is immature at birth.
source: There is also evidence that both the physiology and anatomy of the extrastriate visual system is immature at birth (Zhang et al., 2005; Baldwin et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013; Bourne and Rosa, 2006; Kiorpes and Movshon, 2003, Kiorpes and Movshon, 2004, Kiorpes and Movshon, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The modular organization of IT can be altered by early experience.
source: Further, the modular organization of IT can be altered by early experience (Srihasam et al., 2014; Op de Beeck et al., 2008; Srihasam et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The organization found in neonates must constitute a proto-architecture that subsequently undergoes maturation and refinement as a consequence of postnatal visual experience.
source: Given the extensive anatomical and physiological changes that occur over the first postnatal year, the organization we describe must constitute a proto-architecture that subsequently undergoes maturation and refinement as a consequence of postnatal visual experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the nature of the early organization, based on evidence of continued development.

claim: Neonatal monkeys exhibited a series of hierarchically organized retinotopic maps.
source: Neonatal monkeys exhibited a series of hierarchically organized retinotopic maps.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings about retinotopic organization.

claim: The adult visual cortex contains a series of retinotopic maps; each map comprises a two dimensional gradient of visual field location.
source: The adult visual cortex contains a series of retinotopic maps; each map comprises a two dimensional gradient of visual field location.
evidence: This is established knowledge about adult visual cortex organization.

claim: Correlated activity in neonates varied as a function of visual field representation both along polar angle and eccentricity dimensions.
source: Correlated activity in neonates similarly varied as a function of visual field representation both along polar angle and eccentricity dimensions (Figure 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: In adults, each map in the hierarchy is not just a copy of the preceding map; rather both stimulus selectivity and receptive-field scale increase moving up the hierarchy.
source: In adults, each map in the hierarchy is not just a copy of the preceding map; rather both stimulus selectivity and receptive-field scale increase moving up the hierarchy (Hubel and Wiesel, 1974).
evidence: This is established knowledge about adult visual hierarchy, supported by citation.

claim: Convergence with increasing receptive field scale is an architectural feature of the visual hierarchy in adults that is thought to be an important computational principle underlying both increasing stimulus selectivity and invariance to scale and position.
source: This convergence with increasing receptive field scale is an architectural feature of the visual hierarchy in adults that is thought to be an important computational principle underlying both increasing stimulus selectivity and invariance to scale and position (Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999).
evidence: This is a theoretical framework from previous research, supported by citation.

claim: The hierarchical maps in infants do not reflect a simple serial duplication from one map to the next, matched to scale.
source: The hierarchical maps in infants similarly do not reflect a simple serial duplication from one map to the next, matched to scale
evidence: This is an inference from the spatial frequency mapping data.

claim: The increasing average spatial frequency preference moving up the hierarchy indicates an increase in receptive field scale in infants, as in adults.
source: but the increasing average spatial frequency preference moving up the hierarchy indicates an increase in receptive field scale, as in adults.
evidence: This is an inference from the spatial frequency mapping data.

claim: The scaffolding for hierarchical computations thought to support object recognition is already present at, or emerges shortly after, birth.
source: Thus our data indicate that the scaffolding for hierarchical computations thought to support object recognition is already present at, or emerges shortly after, birth.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings for understanding visual development.

claim: In adult humans and macaques, there is a correspondence between foveal bias and face selectivity and between peripheral bias and scene selectivity.
source: In adult humans and macaques, there is a correspondence between foveal bias and face selectivity and between peripheral bias and scene selectivity (Lafer-Sousa and Conway, 2013; Hasson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Category selectivity emerges in monkeys at around 6 months of age (~200 days).
source: Recently, we found that category selectivity emerges in monkeys at around 6 months of age (~200 days) (Livingstone et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a previous study from the same lab.

claim: The IT regions that eventually become face selective have a foveal bias at birth.
source: Here, we show that the IT regions that eventually become face selective have a foveal bias at birth.
evidence: This is supported by eccentricity correlation analysis of neonatal data.

claim: Spatial frequency tuning, and by extension receptive field properties that scale with eccentricity, was identified throughout visual cortex several months before face clusters emerged.
source: Further, spatial frequency tuning, and by extension receptive field properties that scale with eccentricity, was identified throughout visual cortex several months before face clusters emerged.
evidence: This is supported by spatial frequency mapping at 110 days.

claim: Different parts of IT would have receptive fields that were already differentially selective for low-level stimulus features, before they became selective for higher-level features, such as category.
source: This means that different parts of IT would have receptive fields that were already differentially selective for low-level stimulus features, before they became selective for higher-level features, such as category.
evidence: This is an inference from the spatial frequency and curvature mapping data.

claim: The correlation between eccentricity and receptive-field size, and between eccentricity and curvature means that a retinotopic proto-map is also a proto-map for low-level stimulus features.
source: Thus the correlation between eccentricity and receptive-field size, and between eccentricity and curvature means that a retinotopic proto-map is also a proto-map for low-level stimulus features.
evidence: This is an inference from the relationship between retinotopy and low-level feature selectivity.

claim: Faces differ from most other object categories in being rich in curved contours, whereas scenes are richer in rectilinearity.
source: Faces differ from most other object categories in being rich in curved contours, whereas scenes are richer in rectilinearity (Torralba and Oliva, 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A shape-biased proto-map could contribute to the stereotyped localization of face selectivity to foveal regions of IT.
source: so a shape-biased proto-map could contribute to the stereotyped localization of face selectivity to foveal regions of IT (Srihasam et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about how early organization might influence later category selectivity.

claim: We tend to foveate faces but not scenes.
source: We tend to foveate faces but not scenes
evidence: This is general knowledge about viewing behavior.

claim: Viewing behavior could contribute to the stereotyped localization of category domains.
source: so viewing behavior could also contribute to the stereotyped localization of category domains (Hasson et al., 2002; Levy et al., 2001).
evidence: This is speculation about how viewing behavior might influence category organization, supported by citations.

claim: A retinotopic proto-organization in IT serves as the scaffolding for subsequent category-selective organization, because it carries with it a shape-based organization and/or because of where in the visual field different categories are preferentially experienced.
source: Our data provide novel evidence supporting the hypothesis that a retinotopic proto-organization in IT serves as the scaffolding for subsequent category-selective organization, because it carries with it a shape-based organization and/or because of where in the visual field different categories are preferentially experienced.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: The retinotopic organization of visual cortex emerges very early in development as a consequence of molecular cues and self-organizing principles and serves as scaffolding for further experience-dependent specialization.
source: We propose that the retinotopic organization of visual cortex emerges very early in development as a consequence of molecular cues and self-organizing principles and serves as scaffolding for further experience-dependent specialization.
evidence: This is the main proposal of the paper about the role of early retinotopic organization.

claim: Parallels exist for other sensory areas, and possibly all of cortex, where topographic maps may form the proto-architecture on which experience-dependent specializations are elaborated.
source: At a broader scale, we propose that parallels exist for other sensory areas, and possibly all of cortex. For example, somatotopic organization was also apparent in the newborn data. Thus topographic maps in general may form the proto-architecture of cortex on which experience-dependent specializations are elaborated; this is likely to be a general principle in development.
evidence: This is a broader speculation about cortical development in general, based on the findings in visual cortex and observation of somatotopic organization.
